name: Product Spaces
kick: topology · first principles · gluing one shape's coordinates to another's
title: Product spaces — when a bigger space is just two shapes paired together
lede: Many of the spaces we actually care about are built by taking two simpler things and pairing every point of one with every point of the other. A doughnut is a circle paired with a circle. A robot arm's configuration is its joint angles all multiplied together. Here is how to see a hidden product, and the remarkable fact that the Euler characteristic — that stubborn number from earlier — just multiplies when you build a product.
arc: Many real spaces are really two things at once
The product: pair every point with every point
Seen on a real run — the characteristic multiplies
When a space only looks like a product locally
Where products hide in bigger systems

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — many real spaces are really two things at once

blocks.html: A doughnut's surface is a location on the circle of angles (around the hole) and a location on the circle of angles (around the tube). A cylinder is where you stand on a circle and how high you climb. A robot's arm is joint angle 1 and joint angle 2 and joint angle 3. In physics, a state is position and momentum. In a video, a pixel is a horizontal coordinate and a vertical coordinate and a time. These are not separate things layered on top of each other — they are genuinely one thing seen as a combination of two simpler parts.
So the question is: is there a way to describe a space that is 'one thing AND another' as a single mathematical object, and does it have topological properties we can measure?

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — the product: pair every point with every point

blocks.html: The definition: the product of two spaces A and B is the set of all pairs. You take every point in A and every point in B, and you glue them together as a single entity. A point in the product is literally a pair: (some choice from A, some choice from B).

For example, a circle is all the angles from 0 to 360 degrees. A circle paired with a circle is every way to pick an angle from the first circle (call it the 'around the hole' angle) and an angle from the second circle (call it the 'around the tube' angle). That paired space is the doughnut — the torus. Similarly, a circle paired with an interval (a line segment) is a cylinder: the angle tells you where on the circle, and the height tells you how far up.

This seems almost obvious once you name it. But The key: the Euler characteristic of the product space is just the Euler characteristic of the first space times the characteristic of the second. The number multiplies.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — the characteristic multiplies when you build a product

blocks.html: We computed the Euler characteristic of three product spaces and verified the multiplication rule. A circle has Euler characteristic 0 (as we learned earlier, because you can't comb a circle flat without a tangle). An interval (a line segment) has characteristic 1. A sphere has characteristic 2. blocks.caption: Every product's Euler characteristic is exactly the product of the two parts' characteristics — a fact computed by counting vertices, edges, and faces.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: when you pair two spaces together, the Euler characteristic of the result is exactly the first characteristic times the second. A circle paired with itself (a torus) is 0 times 0, which is 0. A sphere paired with a circle is 2 times 0, which is 0. The number obeys multiplication, not addition. That is a profound constraint: it tells you that any product involving even one space with characteristic 0 (like a circle or torus) will collapse the whole product to 0, no matter what the other part is.

The reason is beautiful and geometric. When you have a product of two spaces, you can tile it by gluing together panels from both. The move: take a tiling of the first space (say, a circle cut into, say, 2 arcs) and a tiling of the second space (say, a circle cut into 3 arcs). The product's natural tiling is a grid: every region of the first gets crossed by every region of the second, so you get 2 times 3 = 6 patches. Each intersection of an edge from the first and an edge from the second gives you a corner in the product. When you compute corners-minus-edges-plus-faces for the product, the alternating sum factors exactly: if the first space has Euler characteristic A and the second has B, the product gets A times B.
In short: the paneling of a product is a Cartesian grid of panels, and the alternating sum on a grid factors like multiplication.
The hidden quantity is how invariants combine: tiling a product of two spaces factorises, so the Euler characteristic of the product is the product of the two separate Euler characteristics.

sections.h2: 5 · The one limit — not every space is a product

blocks.html: Not every shape you draw is secretly a product. A sphere is not a product of two circles — if it were, it would have Euler characteristic 0 times 0 = 0, but it has 2. A Klein bottle (a shape you get if you allow 'twisted' gluings) looks like a product locally, but globally it is not — the twist prevents you from finding a consistent way to pair up coordinates everywhere at once.

Recognizing when a space is actually a product and which two shapes are doing the pairing is a real topological skill. Many spaces look like products near each point (we call them locally a product) but turn out to be woven differently at the larger scale. Finding the hidden product in a complicated space is the kind of problem that dominates differential geometry and theoretical physics — where you ask, 'Is this configuration space really built from two things, or is there a subtlety I missed?'

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — products are everywhere in the real world

blocks.html: A robot arm with three joints has a configuration space that is a product of three circles — one for each joint angle. The space of all possible orientations (rotations) in 3D space is not quite a product, but it is built from products in a way that controls how the robot can move.

In physics, the space of all 'states' of a system is a product: every particle has a position (a point in space) and a momentum (a direction and speed). The whole state space is position times momentum — called 'phase space'. Equations of motion (like Newton's laws or quantum Schrödinger evolution) move points around in this product space. The fact that the Euler characteristic multiplies means that if even one factor has characteristic 0, the whole phase space does too — a constraint that shows up in conservation laws and symmetry principles.

Computer vision sees products everywhere: a video is space times time; an image is pixels across times pixels down. A sensor reading is measurement 1 and measurement 2 and measurement 3, all paired as a single state. Every high-dimensional 'space of possibilities' — whether it is parameters in a neural network, states in a search, or configurations in a manufacturing plant — is built by taking many simpler factors and multiplying them together.

The humbling lesson: most spaces you bump into are secretly products, and the Euler characteristic tells you the cost of that structure. A number multiplies. That is topology's claim on how things compose.

sections.h2: 7 · Where it is used in practice — When one shape is really two shapes paired

blocks.html: A robot arm's control space is each joint angle paired with every other joint angle. A video is horizontal position paired with vertical position paired with time. A system's state is its location paired with its momentum. DNA transcription uses configuration space where one degree of freedom pairs with another. Phase space in physics pairs position with velocity for every particle.

Instead of thinking of the whole space as one messy thing, factor it: 'This is circle-times-circle' or 'interval-times-circle.' Once you see the product structure, the topology multiplies: the Euler count of the product is just the count of one space times the count of the other. This multiplication is rigid—if either space has count zero, the product collapses to zero too. Robots and physicists use this to prove constraints on what motion is possible.
Most complex spaces split into paired factors, and the Euler number obeys multiplication, not addition.

recipe.summary: Compute Euler characteristic (vertices minus edges plus faces) for three product spaces: circle × circle (torus), circle × interval (cylinder), sphere × circle. Verify chi(A × B) = chi(A) × chi(B) for each product.
recipe.eq:
chi(A × B) = chi(A) × chi(B)
# circle: chi = 0
# interval: chi = 1
# sphere: chi = 2
# circle × circle = 0 × 0 = 0
# circle × interval = 0 × 1 = 0
# sphere × circle = 2 × 0 = 0
